overview: Babylonia was a southern Mesopotamian region centred on Babylon, not one dynasty with a thousand-year reign. Its cities, temples and written records survived Kassite rule, Assyrian domination and a brief Neo-Babylonian empire. The atlas shows only selected snapshots from 1500 to 500 BCE; it omits Babylon’s earlier rise under Hammurabi and continues after Persian conquest in 539 BCE. The map dates describe coverage, not uninterrupted independence.

sections.title: Kingdoms, wars and things they built

items.text: Babylon had become a major capital under Hammurabi in the eighteenth century BCE, before this map’s first Babylonian snapshot. The Hittite raid of 1595 BCE ended his dynasty, but did not erase the city. Kassite rulers later adopted many Babylonian political and religious traditions while governing a new territorial state.

Around the late fifteenth or early fourteenth century BCE, Kurigalzu I built Dur-Kurigalzu, a city with temples and a palace. Kassite rulers exchanged messages and goods with courts from Egypt to Anatolia. Their artisans experimented with molded and glazed brick, a technique later used spectacularly at Babylon.

Kassite kings recorded land gifts on stone monuments called kudurrus. A later example shows a dragon associated with Marduk and symbols of several gods. Despite the modern nickname ‘boundary stones,’ these records were probably kept in temples rather than planted in farm fields. Ancient paperwork could be impressive stonework.

An Elamite army ended Kassite rule around 1155 BCE and carried away sacred objects, including Marduk’s statue. Nebuchadnezzar I later recovered that statue. In the following centuries Assyrian kings dominated Babylonia; uprisings continued, and Sennacherib sacked Babylon in 689 BCE.

Nabopolassar’s dynasty broke Assyrian power and built the Neo-Babylonian empire. Nebuchadnezzar II raised walls, gates and temples at Babylon. The Ishtar Gate’s approach was lined with bright glazed lions; those striking animals were part of a ceremonial route, not evidence that real lions wandered the street on festival day.

Clay archives from Babylonian cities record land, goods and agreements from temples and private households. They make everyday economic life visible far beyond royal monuments. The surviving sample favours people whose transactions were written down, so it cannot describe every worker or family equally.

At Borsippa, priests’ archives name bakers, brewers, butchers and oxherds who supplied four meals a day for the god Nabû. The oxen were managed by a family actually called the Oxherds. Even the divine menu required very human work: preparing food, caring for animals and guarding gates.

Borsippa’s temple jobs could belong to families for generations, with a share in temple service and rules of lineage and ritual purity. That tells us about one privileged, well-documented social world, not every Babylonian household. The tablets also reveal personal lives behind the official work rosters.

Babylonia’s New Year festival brought Marduk’s statue from the Esagila temple along the Processional Way, accompanied by visiting gods’ statues. A king ceremonially took the god’s hand. The event linked religious devotion with public power and turned the decorated city route into a stage for a major gathering.

One small Old Babylonian school tablet fits in a hand. A teacher wrote a cuneiform model and a student copied it on the other side; on this tablet, the name of the god Urash appears six times. A student who had to repeat a sign has something in common with children practising handwriting today.

Old Babylonian trainee scribes also copied model contracts covering loans, land sales, marriage and adoption. These were practice pieces, not legally binding deals. Learning to write meant learning the formulas that made business and family agreements work in a document-heavy society.

Mesopotamian medical texts included lists of symptoms and predicted outcomes as well as instructions using plants and minerals. Healers could combine practical treatments with religious ideas. Surviving tablets tell us what specialists wrote, not how often remedies helped or whether every family could obtain them.

A royal inscription of Nebuchadnezzar II contains ‘LUGAL KÁ.DINGIR.RA.KI,’ meaning ‘king of Babylon.’ These are the editor’s Roman-letter signs for Akkadian cuneiform, not a claim that the king wrote in Latin letters. The original wedge marks were impressed or inscribed into a physical object; the transliteration lets us see the words accurately here.

ending.text: Cyrus II of Persia captured Babylon in 539 BCE, ending the Neo-Babylonian empire. The city and its temples continued under Persian rule, while scholars still wrote religious, literary and scholarly works in Akkadian. The atlas’s 500 BCE cutoff is a map limit, not the disappearance of Babylonian people or learning.
